gloss.4: zhé: blame, a fault that brings punishment

zh.text: 善閉無關楗而不可開，善結無繩約而不可解。

gloss.3: the wooden bar across a door; also a frontier pass
gloss.14: a binding; also a treaty, a sworn agreement

gloss.6: to stop harm; to come to the aid of

zh.text: 常善救物，故無棄物。是謂襲明。故善人者，不善人之師；

gloss.12: to wear one robe over another; to inherit; to follow

gloss.2: the essential point; first: the waist

rendering: Good speaking has no [[flaw to blame|xia-zhe]].
Good shutting has no [[bar or bolt|guan-jian]],
Good tying has no [[cord or binding|sheng-yue]],
So [[the sage|shengren]] is always good at [[coming to people’s aid|jiu]],
and so there is [[no discarded person|qi]];
always good at coming to the aid of things,
and so there is no discarded thing.
This is called [[light under a robe|xi-ming]].
So the good person is the not-good person’s [[teacher|shi-zi]].
[[The not-good person|shan-bushan]] is the good person’s [[material|zi]].
Not to prize the teacher, not to care for the material:

shan.title: 善, eleven times
shan.body: The passage uses one word eleven times, and the word changes under the reader’s eyes. In the first five lines 善 means “good at”: skilled at walking, at speech, at counting, at shutting, at tying. In the middle it is the sage’s skill with people. In the last stanza it has become “the good person” and “the not-good person”, which sounds moral. English has two words, “skilled” and “good”, and must change horses in the middle. Chinese does not. The old character, 譱, has a sheep, 羊, between two 言, “speech”; the Shuowen glosses it 吉也, “auspicious”, and says that it has the same idea as 義, right, and 美, fine. So goodness here is closer to a craft that turns out well than to obedience to a rule. If “good” and “good at it” were one word for you, whom would you call good?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 誩部: 譱，吉也。从誩从羊。此與義美同意。

zhe-ji.title: 轍 and 迹: wheel and foot
zhe-ji.body: Two kinds of trace. 轍 has 車, a chariot; the Shuowen says 車迹也, “the track of a cart”. 迹 has the walking sign; the Shuowen says 步處也, “the place of a step”. So 行 in this line covers riding and walking. In the Warring States period ruts were a practical matter: the carts of different states are said to have had different axle widths, each wearing its own grooves into the roads, and in 221 BCE the First Emperor ordered one gauge for all carts. A rut records every earlier traveller and forces the next one into the same line. Wang Bi explains how one could leave none: 順自然而行，不造不始, “travel in accord with what is so of itself; do not make, do not initiate”. The line does not say that the good traveller hides the tracks. There are none. What have you done that left no groove for the next person to fall into?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 車部: 轍，車迹也。从車，徹省聲。
Shuowen Jiezi, 辵部: 迹，步處也。从辵亦聲。
Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 27
Shiji 6, “Basic Annals of the First Emperor”

xia-zhe.title: Speech that cannot be punished
xia-zhe.body: 瑕 is written with 玉, jade: it is a flaw or stain in the stone. 讁 is written with 言, speech; the Shuowen lists it in the form 謫 and glosses it 罰也, “to punish”. So the line pairs a blemish with its penalty. This was not a figure of speech for the first readers. A travelling adviser lived by his tongue at courts where one wrong phrase could end a career or a life. The Han Feizi has a whole essay, “The Difficulties of Persuasion”, on how a speaker dies: he touches the ruler’s secret, or praises the wrong man, or is right too early. Good speech, in this line, is not eloquence. It offers no edge for blame to catch on. The Mawangdui copies are reported to write 瑕適, a sound-loan for the same word. Can you say a true thing so that it leaves nothing to seize?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 言部: 謫，罰也。从言啻聲。
Han Feizi, “Shui nan”
Mawangdui Laozi, silk texts A and B (as reported)

chou-ce.title: Counting rods
chou-ce.body: Before the abacus, Chinese arithmetic was done with small rods laid out on a mat or table. Both 籌 and 策 have 竹, bamboo, on top. The Shuowen describes the tool under another character, 筭: 長六寸。計歷數者, “six inches long; that with which one calculates the calendar and numbers”, and adds that because the rods are always handled, 弄, there are no mistakes. The rods stood upright for units and lay flat for tens, in turn, so the system was already decimal and positional. 策 also names the yarrow stalks that were counted out to consult the Book of Changes. So the tool was used both to reckon and to divine. Wang Bi says of the good counter: 因物之數，不假形也, “follows the number that things themselves have, and borrows no outward form”. Think of a shepherd who knows that one is missing without counting. What do you know that way?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 竹部: 筭，長六寸。計歷數者。从竹从弄。言常弄乃不誤也。
Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 27

guan-jian.title: 關 and 楗: the bar and the pin
guan-jian.body: A Chinese gate was locked from inside with wood. The Shuowen defines 關 as 以木橫持門戶也, “a timber set across to hold the door leaves”, and 楗 as 限門也, the piece that stops the door. For 閉, “to shut”, it explains the small shape inside the gate as 所以歫門也, “that which blocks the door”. The silk copies are reported to say 不可啟 where ours says 不可開: 啟 was the personal name of Emperor Jing of Han (ruled 157–141 BCE), and later copyists could not write it. The word 關 grew: from a door bar to a fortified pass on a frontier, where a state shut out its neighbours. Legend places the birth of this book at such a pass. Sima Qian tells that the keeper of the pass asked the old man who was leaving the country to write down his teaching first. A book about doors that need no bar was, in the story, written at a barred gate.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 門部: 關，以木橫持門戶也。 閉，闔門也。从門；才，所以歫門也。
Shuowen Jiezi, 木部: 楗，限門也。从木建聲。
Shiji 63, “Biography of Laozi”

sheng-yue.title: 約: a knot, a treaty
sheng-yue.body: 繩 is a rope. 約 is “to wind round and bind”; the Shuowen says 纏束也, and both characters have 糸, silk thread. But 約 was also the daily word for a sworn agreement between states, and 結, “to tie”, was the verb for making one. The fourth century BCE was full of such knots. States swore covenants over the blood of a sacrificed animal, formed the “vertical” league against Qin and the “horizontal” league with it, and broke them within a season. A reader of that time heard politics in this line: the good bond needs no oath and no hostage, and it holds. The Zhuangzi has a close parallel: things in their constant state are bound together 不以纆索, “not by ropes”; and the Mawangdui copies of our line are reported to write 纆約, with the same word for rope. What holds you to the people you would not leave?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 糸部: 約，纏束也。从糸勺聲。
Zhuangzi 8, “Webbed Toes”
Mawangdui Laozi, silk texts A and B (as reported)

wb-five.title: Wang Bi: five skills, one rule
wb-five.body: Wang Bi sums up the five opening lines in one sentence: 此五者皆言不造不施，因物之性，不以形制物也。 “These five all speak of not making and not applying: of following the nature of things, and not ruling things by forms.” 形 is outward shape: a visible device, a rule, a tool laid on from outside. The rut, the checked phrase, the rod, the bolt, and the cord are all 形. Each is a sign that the work did not fit the thing and had to be held in place. The door that fits its frame does not need the bar. This is his reading of 無為 as craft, and it is close to the cook in the Zhuangzi who cuts up an ox for nineteen years with one knife, because the blade goes where the gaps already are. Where in your work is there a bolt that covers for a bad fit?
src: Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 27
Zhuangzi 3, “The Secret of Caring for Life”

shengren.title: The sage as a craftsman
shengren.body: 聖人 is “the sage”, and the English word misleads. This is not a saint, who is holy, and not only a wise man, who knows much. The Shuowen glosses 聖 as 通也, “open, getting through”, and the character has an ear in it. In this passage the sage comes after five craftsmen, joined by 是以, “and so”: the sage is the sixth craftsman, and the material is people and things. Note also 常, “always”. The Mawangdui copies are reported to write 恆, the older word that a Han taboo later removed (see passage 1). The sage’s skill is steady, like a trade that someone has practised for a lifetime. The text does not say that the sage loves everyone. It says that the sage is good at something. Does that seem a lower claim to you, or a higher one?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 耳部: 聖，通也。从耳呈聲。
Mawangdui Laozi, silk texts A and B (as reported)

jiu.title: 救 is not “to save”
jiu.body: The Shuowen defines 救 in one word: 止也, “to stop”. The right side of the character, 攵, is a hand with a stick, a sign of action. To 救 is to step in and halt a harm: to put out a fire, relieve a besieged town, pull a child from a well. Armies were sent to 救 an ally. English “save” carries a second meaning from the churches: to rescue a soul from sin for another life, and [[Legge|legge]] writes “saving men”. Nothing here concerns souls. The sage’s skill is practical and present: no one is left in the ditch. And the object is not only people. The next line says 救物, to come to the aid of things: tools, animals, scraps, land. The Mawangdui copies are reported to put it another way, with no second “always good at”: 而无棄人，物无棄財, “and no person is thrown away; among things, no goods are thrown away”.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 攴部: 救，止也。从攴求聲。
Mawangdui Laozi, silk texts A and B (as reported)

qi.title: 棄: a child in a basket
qi.body: The word for “discard” has a hard picture in it. The Shuowen analyses 棄 as two hands, 廾, that push a winnowing basket to throw something out, and on top a part that it explains as 逆子也: “a child, upside down”. The oldest forms are commonly described the same way: an infant, a basket, two hands. To 棄 was first to expose a newborn. The founding ancestor of the Zhou royal house was named for it. He was Hou Ji, Lord Millet, whose personal name was 棄, “the Abandoned”: an ode tells how his mother left him in a lane, in a forest, and on ice, and each time oxen, woodcutters, or birds kept him alive. So when the text says 無棄人, “no discarded person”, the character on the page is a baby that someone is throwing away. Who, in your world, is in the basket?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 𠦒部: 棄，捐也。从廾推𠦒棄之，从𠫓。𠫓，逆子也。
Shijing, Da ya, “Sheng min” (生民)
Shiji 4, “Basic Annals of Zhou”

wb-qi.title: Wang Bi: who makes the rejects?
wb-qi.body: Wang Bi asks how anyone comes to be discarded, and his answer is institutional: 聖人不立形名以檢於物，不造進向以殊棄不肖。 “The sage does not set up forms and names to check things against, and does not create goals to advance toward, by which the unworthy are singled out and discarded.” In his view the reject is produced by the standard. Set up a title and a test, and at once some people are those who failed it. He then quotes passage 3: do not exalt the worthy, and the people do not contend. This is a direct answer to the Legalist method of his text’s own time, 形名, “forms and names”, in which each officer was measured against his title. The sage in this reading does not rescue people one by one from the heap. The sage does not build the heap.
src: Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 27

xi-ming.title: 襲明: three readings of a rare phrase
xi-ming.body: No one is sure what 襲明 means. 襲 has 衣, a garment, under a dragon, 龍, which is short for the sound part 龖, two dragons. The Shuowen’s gloss is 左衽袍, “a robe that closes to the left”: the dress of the dead, since the living closed their robes to the right. From that the word means to put one garment over another; then to inherit, to repeat, to follow; then to fall on an enemy from cover. So 襲明 may be light that is covered, as the good walker’s skill is; or light that is handed on, from teacher to pupil; or “to follow the light”. We chose the first, because the passage began with a skill that shows no trace. Passage 52 has a sister phrase, 襲常. The Mawangdui copies are reported to write 曳明 here, a character that means “to trail, to draw along”; scholars differ on how to take it. Which light do you trust more: shown, or worn under a robe?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 衣部: 襲，左衽袍。从衣，龖省聲。
Mawangdui Laozi, silk texts A and B (as reported)

shi-zi.title: Whose teacher?
shi-zi.body: The received text makes a neat cross: the good person teaches the not-good; the not-good person is material for the good. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to say something else in the first half (text A is damaged here): 故善人，善人之師；不善人，善人之齎也. “So the good person is the good person’s teacher; the not-good person is the good person’s stock.” In that version both lines are about what the good person needs: a model, and material. No one is appointed to instruct the bad. This may be a copyist’s slip, or it may be the older thought, later tidied into a symmetry. The compound that later Chinese made from the two words, 師資, came to mean a teacher, and then “teaching staff”. A phrase that once named two people on opposite sides of a lesson now names one side only. What was lost when the material dropped out of the word?
src: Mawangdui Laozi, silk texts A and B (as reported)

zi.title: 資: stock, capital, raw material
zi.body: 資 has 貝, the cowrie shell of early money, at the bottom. The Shuowen glosses it 貨也, “goods”. It is what a trader has to work with: stock, capital, supplies. Wang Bi explains it by a verb: 資，取也, “資 is to take from”. So the line is blunt. The not-good person is what the good person draws on, as a carpenter draws on timber. Read one way, this is hard: people as material. Read the other way, it is humble: a carpenter with no timber is not a carpenter, and the skilled have their skill only because the unskilled are there to be met. The next line settles the tone with the verb 愛, “to care for, to hold dear”. One does not hold dear a thing that one merely uses up. Who has been your material, and did you care for them?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 貝部: 資，貨也。从貝次聲。
Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 27

da-mi.title: 迷: lost on the road
da-mi.body: 迷 has the walking sign 辶 round 米, which gives the sound. The Shuowen glosses it with 或, here the old way to write 惑, “to be in doubt, led astray”. It is the word for a traveller who has lost the road. The silk copies are reported to write 大眯; the Shuowen glosses 眯 as 艸入目中也, “grass has got into the eye”. The passage began with good walking that leaves no rut, and it ends with a clever person on foot and far off the way. The word before 大迷 is 智: knowledge, cleverness. In this book that word is usually a warning (passages 18, 19, 65). Wang Bi names the fault: 自任其智，不因物, “relies on his own cleverness and does not follow things”. The size word matters too: 大迷, “greatly lost”. A fool is lost in a small way and may ask. The clever person is lost at speed, and with a map. Have you been lost like that?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 辵部: 迷，或也。从辵米聲。
Shuowen Jiezi, 目部: 眯，艸入目中也。从目米聲。
Mawangdui Laozi, silk texts A and B (as reported)
Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 27

yao-miao.title: 要妙: the waist of the matter
yao-miao.body: 要 was first the waist. The Shuowen says 身中也, “the middle of the body”, and describes the character as a person with both hands at the waist; the body sense is now written 腰. The waist is where the body turns and where a belt gathers a robe, so 要 came to mean the point that holds the rest: the essential. 妙 is the fineness of passage 1, the first small stir of a thing. Together: the fine point on which it all turns. The Mawangdui copies are reported to write the two words in the other order, 眇要, with the eye-radical character 眇, “so small that the eye strains”. And what is the crux? Not the five skills, and not the rescue. The passage gives its name to the last pair: the teacher prized, the material held dear. The secret that it promises is a relation between two people.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 𦥑部: 要，身中也。象人要自𦥑之形。
Shuowen Jiezi, 目部: 眇，一目小也。从目从少，少亦聲。
Mawangdui Laozi, silk texts A and B (as reported)

legge.title: Legge and the “man of skill”
legge.body: Legge renders 善 as “skilful” all the way through, even at the end: “the man of skill is a master”. This is consistent, and it protects the English reader from a sermon about good and bad people. But see what he does with the two relations. The not-good one becomes “the helper of (the reputation of) him who has the skill”. The bracket turns the material into an audience: the unskilled make the skilled look good. And the warning line becomes a remark about a third party, an “(observer)” who “might greatly err about them”. The Chinese has no observer and no reputation. It says that the one who fails to prize the teacher or to care for the material is lost. He also gives 襲明 as “Hiding the light of his procedure”, which adds a method to a phrase that has none. Why might a Victorian need the bystander?
src: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (1891)

shan-bushan.title: 善 and 不善: each is made from the other
shan-bushan.body: The last stanza sets two people side by side: 善人 and 不善人, the one good at it and the one not good at it. English hears a saint and a sinner, and then the lines rank them: one above to teach, one below to be worked on. The Chinese ties them with two nouns, 師 and 資, and both nouns are debts. The not-good person needs a [[teacher|shi-zi]]. The good person needs [[material|zi]], and with no material there is no skill and no teacher. Each is what the other is made from. The next line asks the same of both sides: 貴 the teacher, 愛 the material. And the pair moves. The pupil of today teaches later; a master of one craft is raw stock in the next. 不善 is “not good”, with 不; it is not “bad”. So the sage [[discards no one|qi]]. In which room are you the material?

lenses.ground: Three parts. First, five trades, each in one line: travel, speech, reckoning, door-making, binding. Each is said to be [[good|shan]] when its usual tool or trace is absent: no [[rut|zhe-ji]], no [[blemish|xia-zhe]], no [[rods|chou-ce]], no [[bar|guan-jian]], no [[rope|sheng-yue]]. The last two add a boast: and yet no one can open it or untie it. Second, 是以, “and so”: [[the sage|shengren]] has the same kind of skill with people and with things, and the result is stated as an absence too: [[no one and nothing thrown away|qi]]. This gets a name, [[襲明|xi-ming]]. Third, a pair: teacher and [[material|zi]], each owed something, and a warning that cleverness does not help the one who forgets that debt. This also gets a name, [[要妙|yao-miao]]. Wang Bi reads the whole first part as [[one rule|wb-five]].
lenses.inner: The five skills describe action that comes from fit and not from force. When attention is whole, a thing is done and nothing is left over: no [[track of self-regard|zhe-ji]], no after-thought to defend, no tally of who owes whom. The contemplative traditions call this many things; this passage calls it [[light under a robe|xi-ming]], clarity that does not need to be seen. The second half turns the same eye inward. Each person holds a good one and a not-good one. If the part that sees clearly despises the part that fails, the result is [[“greatly lost”|da-mi]], with all one’s cleverness intact. The failed part is the [[material|zi]]. It is what practice is made of. The text asks for two feelings, in order: respect for what teaches, and affection for what is taught. [[No part is put out in the basket.|qi]]
lenses.leading: Wang Bi’s comment turns this into a question about systems: [[rejects are made by standards|wb-qi]]. Any organisation that ranks people creates a bottom rank and then has to decide what to do with it. The passage offers another picture of a group: someone good at a thing, someone not yet good at it, and a bond between them that runs both ways. The one who knows is owed honour. The one who does not know is owed care, and is also the reason the first one has a function at all. The five opening lines apply to management directly. A team that needs [[many bolts|guan-jian]] (approvals, contracts, surveillance) is showing that its doors do not fit. [[A bond that holds without a cord|sheng-yue]] is slower to make and cannot be ordered. In the silk copies, as reported, even the good person [[needs a teacher|shi-zi]].
lenses.body: Watch someone who is truly good at a physical craft: a mason, a cook, a calligrapher. The movement is small and nothing is corrected afterwards. The beginner leaves marks everywhere: chips, spills, strokes gone over twice. Skill in the body is the removal of the extra motion, until the act [[leaves no rut|zhe-ji]]. The door lines can be felt in a joint. A well-set shoulder or hip is closed by its own shape and needs no clenched muscle to hold it; a clenched one is a [[bolt|guan-jian]], and it can be forced. The tying line is known to anyone who has learned a real knot: the good one holds by its form and comes apart when you want, and the bad one is a tangle with much rope in it. [[Good at|shan]] is first a thing that hands know.
lenses.practice: Choose one small task today and do it so that it leaves no trace of you: wash a cup and put it away, close a matter with one clear sentence, return a borrowed thing in better order than you got it. Do not mention it to anyone. That is the first stanza. For the second, look for one [[discarded thing|qi]] in your house or your work (a tool, a draft, a plant, a person who has been written off) and ask what it would take to bring it back into use; do one step of that. For the third, name privately one person who is your teacher and one who is your [[material|zi]]. Ask if you prize the first and hold the second dear. If the second answer is no, the text has [[a word for your position|da-mi]].

questions.claim: For one who is truly skilled at helping, no person and no thing is waste.
prompts: Do you believe that? Think of a person you have written off, and ask it again.
Where did you learn who counts as waste: at school, at work, in your family? Were you at some time the one set aside?
Hold the opposite for a time: some people and things must be let go, and to refuse is pride. What do you feel as you hold it?
Which view do you use on others, and which on yourself? Are they the same?

questions.claim: The skilled and the unskilled need each other, and to despise either one is to be lost.
prompts: Do you agree that the one who teaches needs the one who cannot yet do it? Where have you seen it?
Whom do you find it hard to respect: those who know more than you, or those who know less? What in your past makes that side hard?
Now try the other view: the skilled owe nothing to the unskilled, and do best among their own kind. Sit with it. What thoughts and feelings arrive?
What does your reaction tell you about how you see your own skill?

questions.claim: Good work leaves no track, and needs no lock or knot to hold it.
prompts: Is this your experience of good work, your own or another person’s?
How much do you need your work to be seen and signed? Where does that need come from?
Take the opposite: a life should leave marks, and work that no one can trace is lost. Hold that for a while and notice what it stirs.
Which of the two would you choose for your name after you are gone, and why?

plates.title: The teacher is an army
plates.lesson: This character means “teacher” in the passage, and it did not start there. The Shuowen’s first words are a troop count: 二千五百人爲師, “two thousand five hundred men make a 師”. It is a division of the Zhou army. The Shuowen reads the two halves as 帀, “all round”, and 𠂤, and says that together they give 眾意, “the idea of a multitude”. 𠂤 is in its account a small mound; modern scholars debate what the early form shows, and in the oldest inscriptions 𠂤 alone already writes the word for an army in the field. Follow the meaning as it grew. A host of men; then the capital, where the hosts are (京師); then the one who leads and trains a host, a master; then the master of any art: a music master, a teacher. The same thing happened to its cousin 官. The Shuowen says of that character: 𠂤猶眾也。此與師同意, “𠂤 is like ‘the many’; it has the same idea as 師”. An official is one who has charge of many under a roof. Other cousins by 𠂤: 追, to pursue, and 歸, to return, where the Shuowen takes it as the sound. So Chinese remembers that teaching began as command of a crowd. This passage quietly changes the word: its 師 has one pupil, called [[material|zi]], and owes that pupil care. In passage 30 the same character is back in armour: 師之所處, “where the army camps”, thorns grow.
plates.brush: Ten strokes. The left half first. Stroke one is a short stroke at the top that falls to the left. Stroke two is a long vertical from under it down the left edge. Stroke three is a horizontal that turns down: the top and right side of a small upper box. Stroke four is a horizontal that closes that box. Stroke five turns in the same way to make a second box under the first, and stroke six closes it. Now the right half. Stroke seven is a horizontal across the top. Stroke eight is a short vertical on the left of the lower part. Stroke nine is a horizontal that turns down and ends in a hook to the left. Stroke ten is the long vertical through the centre of the right half; it comes last and goes lowest, like a standard set in the ground. In seal script both halves are made of curved lines; the two small boxes are a product of the brush.

plates.title: A sheep and what is said
plates.lesson: At the top of 善 is a sheep, 羊: two horns, then three bars and an upright for the head and body. The Shuowen says of 羊 that it shows 頭角足尾之形, “head, horns, feet, and tail”, and glosses the animal as 祥也, “a good omen”. The full old character is 譱: the sheep stands between two 言, “speech”. The Shuowen gives that pair as a word in its own right, 誩, 競言也, “speech in dispute”. What a sheep does between two parties who argue is not explained; a common account is that the sheep was the offering, or the sign of a lucky outcome, at a settlement. The Shuowen says only 吉也, “auspicious”, and adds a key remark: 此與義美同意, “this has the same idea as 義 and 美”. So meet the family. 美, “beautiful, fine”: sheep over 大, a person face-on; the Shuowen says 甘也, “sweet”, because the sheep is the chief of the six animals for the table. 義, “right, duty”: sheep over 我, “I”. 祥, “omen”: the altar sign beside a sheep. 養, “to feed, to rear”: food with a sheep for the sound. 羣, “flock”: the Shuowen has 羊 under 君, a lord. The good, the fine, and the right all begin with one useful, mild animal. In the modern character the two speeches have shrunk to a few strokes and a mouth. [[The word still means “good at” before it means “good”.|shan]]
plates.brush: Twelve strokes. The first two are the horns: a dot that leans right, then a short stroke that leans left, tips apart, feet together. The third, fourth, and fifth are three horizontals; in a good hand the fifth is longer than the two above it. The sixth is the vertical that runs down through all three. The seventh and eighth repeat the horns in small: a dot and a short left-falling stroke, set under the sheep. The ninth is the longest horizontal in the character; everything above rests on it. Then the mouth: the tenth stroke is its left side, the eleventh its top and right side in one turn, the twelfth the base that closes it. The danger is height. Five horizontals and a box are stacked in one square, so each layer must be thin and the gaps even. In running script the lower horns and the long line fuse into one zigzag.
